headline: Japan Plants 680,000 Trees to Shield Coasts From Tsunamis
meta_description: The Chinju no Mori Project uses fast-growing forests alongside seawalls to protect Japanese coastal communities from tsunami damage, drawing on centuries of na…
summary_short: A Japanese initiative has planted 680,000 trees along vulnerable coastlines using proven forest-growing methods, offering a natural complement to concrete seawalls.
body:
More than 1,000 volunteers gathered on the beaches of Minamisoma, a coastal city in Fukushima prefecture, to plant 12,000 trees on a single day—part of a 14-year effort that has transformed how Japan thinks about tsunami protection. The Chinju no Mori Project, also known as the Morino Project, has planted 680,000 trees along Japan's coastline, creating what organizers call a "wall of trees" to work alongside traditional seawalls. Rather than relying on concrete barriers alone, the initiative draws on centuries of Japanese wisdom and modern forestry science to build natural disaster resilience.

The project's success rests on the Miyawaki method, a planting technique that creates dense, fast-growing forests by crowding together more than 20 varieties of trees and shrubs. As they compete for sunlight, the plants grow taller and stronger, developing into robust barriers that can absorb tsunami energy. This approach was inspired by the "guardian forests" long maintained around Shinto shrines, many of which protected those sacred spaces during the catastrophic 2011 earthquake and tsunami that killed more than 19,700 people across northeastern Japan's 2,000-kilometer coastline.

Research comparing tsunami damage across 130 years of records supports this dual approach. While tall seawalls (over 5 meters) provide the strongest protection, coastal forests also significantly reduce death and destruction by either breaking wave force or discouraging construction in high-risk zones. Yet most Japanese coastal towns continue to prioritize concrete defenses. The volunteers who traveled hundreds of kilometers to plant trees in Minamisoma represent a growing recognition that nature, combined with engineering, offers the most resilient path forward.
quick_facts: 680,000 trees planted over 14 years along Japanese coasts
Minamisoma event: 1,000+ volunteers planted 12,000 trees in one day
2011 tsunami killed 19,700+ people across northeastern Japan
Miyawaki method uses 20+ tree varieties in tight arrangement
Guardian forests around Shinto shrines survived 2011 tsunami
